Data science is a field that uses mathematical algorithms and scientific methods to exract meaningfull data from the unstructured collection.
It is the process of turning raw data into deployment.

Data science began evolving between 1980 and 2000, transitioning from traditional statistics to modern AI-driven systems. Before 2000, it was primarily based on Excel and statistical methods. Between 2000 and 2010, it shifted toward databases and big data technologies. The most recent phase focuses on machine learning and AI.
Generally there are four roles in Data science Data analyst, Data scientist, Data engineer and ML engineer.
Data analyst: Data analyst is the one who collect data, clean data, analyse data and make data usefull for the organisation which can help to take better, and data driven decision.

Data Scientist: Data analyst and scientist both roles works with the data but there is bit of difference data analyst mostly work on historical data to solve specific current problems but data scientist uses advance model to predict future outcomes. Data scientist uses tools like python, tensorflow, R, Spark whereas analyst uses tools like Excel, PwerBi, Tablue and Power Bi etc.
Data scientist basically create machine learning models to find patterns and make prediction from data.

Data Engineer: Data engineer is the one who deals with the systems not exactly with data, they create and maintain system which collect, analyse and store data. They creates pipelines means means automatic data flow system and collect data from different sources like apis, databases and apps.
ML Engineer: An ML engineer is a developer who takes ML model from data scientist and then they optimise it deploy it and monitor it's performance.

So, we are going to start from the very basics: how HTTPS works, the difference between HTTP and HTTPS, what DNS is, what a client and a server are, and how they interact with each other. We will also explore the different ways to establish a connection between a client and a server, along with concepts like scaling, caching, and much more. By the end of this, we aim to think like high-level system engineers.
So, why do we generally prefer HTTPS over HTTP? Maybe HTTPS looks cool? 😂

It's not exactly; let's discuss the configuration of both. Start with http so it works with the plain text, no complexity, faster to send and receive responses, but unsafe. While HTTPS is a combination of HTTP and TLS (Transport Layer Security), it is one step ahead of HTTP. It makes a proper handshake between the client and server to make the data completely safe. And it sends data to the server in encrypted form so that if someone is able to track the request by any chance, there will be encrypted data in the request.
Let's understand the flow of DNS
DNS is basically a distributed system and a protocol that converts the human-searchable text into the IP address.

So, let’s understand how DNS works with an example. Suppose you visit a site like"https://apihub.digital. Initially, the browser checks whether it already knows the IP address. If not, the request goes to a DNS resolver, which resolves the domain name and returns the corresponding IP address to the browser. Then, using that IP address, the browser sends a new request to the specific server. Finally, the server responds with the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, which the browser renders as the web page you see.

1. What is HTML?

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is used to create the structure of web pages. It defines what content is a heading, paragraph, image, link, or form. HTML does not handle styling or logic, only structure and meaning.
2. What is the difference between HTML and HTML5?

HTML5 is the modern version of HTML which introduces semantic tags, multimedia support like audio and video, new input types, local storage, and better mobile support. It also uses a simplified DOCTYPE declaration.
3. What are tags in HTML?
Tags are predefined keywords enclosed in angle brackets that tell the browser how to display content. Example: <p>, <h1>, <img>. Tags usually come in pairs except self-closing tags.
4. What is an HTML element?
An HTML element consists of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag. Example: <p>Hello</p>. The complete structure together is called an element.
5. What is DOCTYPE and why is it important?
DOCTYPE tells the browser which version of HTML is being used. It ensures the browser renders the page in standards mode. Without DOCTYPE, browsers may behave unpredictably.
6. What happens if DOCTYPE is missing?
If DOCTYPE is missing, the browser may enter quirks mode, which can cause layout inconsistencies and CSS issues across different browsers.
Semantic HTML
7. What are semantic HTML elements?
Semantic elements clearly describe their meaning to both browser and developer. Examples include header, nav, section, article, and footer.
8. Why are semantic tags important?
Semantic tags improve SEO, accessibility, and code readability. Search engines and screen readers can better understand the page structure.
9. Difference between semantic and non-semantic tags?
Semantic tags provide meaning (<article>, <header>), while non-semantic tags like <div> and <span> are used only for grouping without meaning.
Block vs Inline Elements
10. What are block-level elements?
Block-level elements start on a new line and take full width available. Examples include div, p, h1-h6, section, and article.
11. What are inline elements?
Inline elements do not start on a new line and take only the space required by their content. Examples include span, a, strong, em.
12. Can inline elements contain block elements?
No, inline elements should not contain block-level elements. However, block elements can contain inline elements.
13. Difference between <div> and <span>?
<div> is a block-level container used for layout sections, while <span> is an inline container used to style small parts of text.
HTML Attributes
14. What are HTML attributes?
Attributes provide additional information about HTML elements. They are written in name-value pairs and always placed inside the opening tag.
15. What is the difference between id and class?
id is unique and used for a single element, while class can be applied to multiple elements. id has higher priority in CSS.
16. What are data-* attributes?
Data attributes allow storing custom data in HTML elements which can be accessed using JavaScript. Example: data-user-id='101'.
Links and Images
17. What is anchor tag used for?
Anchor tag is used to create hyperlinks that link pages, sections, email addresses, or phone numbers using the href attribute.
18. What is the purpose of alt attribute in images?
The alt attribute provides alternative text when an image fails to load and helps screen readers understand images. It is important for SEO and accessibility.
19. Is <img> a self-closing tag?
Yes, the img tag is a self-closing tag and does not require a closing tag.
Lists
20. Difference between ul and ol?
ul creates unordered lists with bullet points, while ol creates ordered lists with numbers or letters.
HTML Forms
21. What are HTML forms?
HTML forms are used to collect user input and send it to a server. Forms include input fields, buttons, dropdowns, and text areas.
22. What is the action attribute in form?
The action attribute specifies the URL where the form data will be submitted after the user clicks submit.
23. What is method attribute in form?
The method attribute defines how data is sent to the server. Common methods are GET and POST.
24. Difference between GET and POST?
GET sends data via URL and is less secure, while POST sends data in request body and is more secure. POST is preferred for sensitive data.
25. What is label tag?
Label tag improves accessibility by connecting text with input fields using for and id attributes.
26. Difference between radio and checkbox?
Radio buttons allow only one selection from a group, while checkboxes allow multiple selections.
HTML Tables
27. What are HTML tables used for?
Tables are used to display structured data in rows and columns, such as reports or comparison charts.
28. What is thead and tbody?
thead contains table headings and tbody contains table body data. This separation improves structure and readability.
29. What is colspan and rowspan?
colspan merges multiple columns into one cell, while rowspan merges multiple rows into one cell.
SEO & Accessibility
30. How does HTML help in SEO?
HTML improves SEO using semantic tags, proper heading structure, alt attributes for images, and meta tags.
31. What is accessibility in HTML?
Accessibility ensures websites are usable by people with disabilities using screen readers and assistive technologies.
32. What is the use of meta tags?
Meta tags provide metadata like description, keywords, author, and viewport settings to browsers and search engines.
33. What is viewport meta tag?
Viewport meta tag controls page layout on mobile devices and makes websites responsive.
34. What is canvas in HTML5?
Canvas is used to draw graphics, animations, and games using JavaScript directly on the web page.
35. What is localStorage?
localStorage allows storing data in the browser with no expiration time. Data remains even after browser restart.
36. Difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
localStorage persists data permanently, while sessionStorage stores data only for the current session.
37. What are self-closing tags?
Self-closing tags do not have closing tags. Examples include img, br, hr, input.
38. Can we nest HTML elements?
Yes, HTML elements can be nested, but they must be properly closed and follow correct hierarchy rules.
39. What is the role of <main> tag?
<main> represents the primary content of the page and should be unique. It helps SEO and accessibility.
40. What is the purpose of <nav> tag?
<nav> is used to define navigation links of a website, such as menus and internal page links.

1. What is HTML?

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is used to create the structure of web pages. It defines what content is a heading, paragraph, image, link, or form. HTML does not handle styling or logic, only structure and meaning.
2. What is the difference between HTML and HTML5?

HTML5 is the modern version of HTML which introduces semantic tags, multimedia support like audio and video, new input types, local storage, and better mobile support. It also uses a simplified DOCTYPE declaration.
3. What are tags in HTML?
Tags are predefined keywords enclosed in angle brackets that tell the browser how to display content. Example: <p>, <h1>, <img>. Tags usually come in pairs except self-closing tags.
4. What is an HTML element?
An HTML element consists of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag. Example: <p>Hello</p>. The complete structure together is called an element.
5. What is DOCTYPE and why is it important?
DOCTYPE tells the browser which version of HTML is being used. It ensures the browser renders the page in standards mode. Without DOCTYPE, browsers may behave unpredictably.
6. What happens if DOCTYPE is missing?
If DOCTYPE is missing, the browser may enter quirks mode, which can cause layout inconsistencies and CSS issues across different browsers.
Semantic HTML
7. What are semantic HTML elements?
Semantic elements clearly describe their meaning to both browser and developer. Examples include header, nav, section, article, and footer.
8. Why are semantic tags important?
Semantic tags improve SEO, accessibility, and code readability. Search engines and screen readers can better understand the page structure.
9. Difference between semantic and non-semantic tags?
Semantic tags provide meaning (<article>, <header>), while non-semantic tags like <div> and <span> are used only for grouping without meaning.
Block vs Inline Elements
10. What are block-level elements?
Block-level elements start on a new line and take full width available. Examples include div, p, h1-h6, section, and article.
11. What are inline elements?
Inline elements do not start on a new line and take only the space required by their content. Examples include span, a, strong, em.
12. Can inline elements contain block elements?
No, inline elements should not contain block-level elements. However, block elements can contain inline elements.
13. Difference between <div> and <span>?
<div> is a block-level container used for layout sections, while <span> is an inline container used to style small parts of text.
HTML Attributes
14. What are HTML attributes?
Attributes provide additional information about HTML elements. They are written in name-value pairs and always placed inside the opening tag.
15. What is the difference between id and class?
id is unique and used for a single element, while class can be applied to multiple elements. id has higher priority in CSS.
16. What are data-* attributes?
Data attributes allow storing custom data in HTML elements which can be accessed using JavaScript. Example: data-user-id='101'.
Links and Images
17. What is anchor tag used for?
Anchor tag is used to create hyperlinks that link pages, sections, email addresses, or phone numbers using the href attribute.
18. What is the purpose of alt attribute in images?
The alt attribute provides alternative text when an image fails to load and helps screen readers understand images. It is important for SEO and accessibility.
19. Is <img> a self-closing tag?
Yes, the img tag is a self-closing tag and does not require a closing tag.
Lists
20. Difference between ul and ol?
ul creates unordered lists with bullet points, while ol creates ordered lists with numbers or letters.
HTML Forms
21. What are HTML forms?
HTML forms are used to collect user input and send it to a server. Forms include input fields, buttons, dropdowns, and text areas.
22. What is the action attribute in form?
The action attribute specifies the URL where the form data will be submitted after the user clicks submit.
23. What is method attribute in form?
The method attribute defines how data is sent to the server. Common methods are GET and POST.
24. Difference between GET and POST?
GET sends data via URL and is less secure, while POST sends data in request body and is more secure. POST is preferred for sensitive data.
25. What is label tag?
Label tag improves accessibility by connecting text with input fields using for and id attributes.
26. Difference between radio and checkbox?
Radio buttons allow only one selection from a group, while checkboxes allow multiple selections.
HTML Tables
27. What are HTML tables used for?
Tables are used to display structured data in rows and columns, such as reports or comparison charts.
28. What is thead and tbody?
thead contains table headings and tbody contains table body data. This separation improves structure and readability.
29. What is colspan and rowspan?
colspan merges multiple columns into one cell, while rowspan merges multiple rows into one cell.
SEO & Accessibility
30. How does HTML help in SEO?
HTML improves SEO using semantic tags, proper heading structure, alt attributes for images, and meta tags.
31. What is accessibility in HTML?
Accessibility ensures websites are usable by people with disabilities using screen readers and assistive technologies.
32. What is the use of meta tags?
Meta tags provide metadata like description, keywords, author, and viewport settings to browsers and search engines.
33. What is viewport meta tag?
Viewport meta tag controls page layout on mobile devices and makes websites responsive.
34. What is canvas in HTML5?
Canvas is used to draw graphics, animations, and games using JavaScript directly on the web page.
35. What is localStorage?
localStorage allows storing data in the browser with no expiration time. Data remains even after browser restart.
36. Difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
localStorage persists data permanently, while sessionStorage stores data only for the current session.
37. What are self-closing tags?
Self-closing tags do not have closing tags. Examples include img, br, hr, input.
38. Can we nest HTML elements?
Yes, HTML elements can be nested, but they must be properly closed and follow correct hierarchy rules.
39. What is the role of <main> tag?
<main> represents the primary content of the page and should be unique. It helps SEO and accessibility.
40. What is the purpose of <nav> tag?
<nav> is used to define navigation links of a website, such as menus and internal page links.

Load Balancer in Node.js with MongoDB

This explanation covers the basics of implementing a load balancer with Node.js and MongoDB, focusing on simplicity.

What is a Load Balancer?

⚖️

A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. This ensures no single server becomes overwhelmed, improving responsiveness, availability, and reliability of applications.

Why Use a Load Balancer with Node.js and MongoDB?

  • Scalability: Easily add more Node.js instances to handle increased traffic without downtime.
  • High Availability: If one Node.js server fails, the load balancer can redirect traffic to other healthy servers.
  • Performance: Distributing requests prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck.

Simple Load Balancing Strategy (Round Robin)

A common and straightforward approach is the Round Robin algorithm. In this method, requests are distributed sequentially to each server in a list.

Node.js Implementation (Conceptual)

For a simple Node.js load balancer, you can use a library like 'http-proxy' or implement a basic proxy yourself. The core idea is to maintain a list of your Node.js application servers and cycle through them.

⚙️

Example using 'http-proxy' (simplified):


const http = require('http');
const httpProxy = require('http-proxy');

const servers = [
    { host: 'localhost', port: 3001 },
    { host: 'localhost', port: 3002 },
    { host: 'localhost', port: 3003 }
];

let currentServerIndex = 0;

const proxy = httpProxy.createProxyServer({});

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
    const targetServer = servers[currentServerIndex];
    proxy.web(req, res, { target: `http://${targetServer.host}:${targetServer.port}` });

    // Move to the next server for the next request
    currentServerIndex = (currentServerIndex + 1) % servers.length;
});

const PORT = 8080; // The port your load balancer listens on
server.listen(PORT, () => {
    console.log(`Load balancer listening on port ${PORT}`);
});

Integrating with MongoDB

When using a load balancer with Node.js and MongoDB, it's crucial to consider how your Node.js instances interact with the database.

Scenario Explanation Considerations
Shared MongoDB Instance All Node.js instances connect to a single MongoDB instance or cluster.
  • Simple setup.
  • Potential bottleneck if MongoDB is not scaled.
  • Ensure MongoDB can handle the concurrent connections from all Node.js instances.
MongoDB Sharding/Replication Use MongoDB's built-in features for scalability and high availability. Node.js instances connect to the replica set or sharded cluster.
  • Provides better performance and resilience for your database layer.
  • Node.js applications typically connect to a replica set's primary for writes and can read from secondaries.
Connection Pooling Each Node.js instance should manage its own connection pool to MongoDB.
  • Essential for efficient database access.
  • Prevents overwhelming the MongoDB server with too many individual connections.
  • Libraries like Mongoose handle connection pooling automatically.

Key Takeaways

  • Load balancers are vital for scaling Node.js applications.
  • Round Robin is a simple yet effective load balancing strategy.
  • Ensure your MongoDB setup (sharding, replication) is also scaled to match your Node.js application's needs.
  • Proper connection pooling in Node.js is critical for database performance.
The Wonderful World of Networks: A Visual Journey
Let's dive into how networks, the invisible highways of our digital lives, actually work. We'll focus on IP and IPv6, and how requests zip across them, all with a heavy dose of visuals!
The Basics: What is a Network?
Imagine a bunch of computers wanting to talk to each other. A network is simply the way they connect and exchange information.
Think of it like a postal service for data!
Every device on a network needs a unique address to be found. This is where IP (Internet Protocol) addresses come in.
An IP address is like your home address, but for your device on the internet.
IPv4: The Original Kid on the Block
IPv4 addresses are the ones you're probably most familiar with. They look like this:
They use 32 bits, which gives us about 4.3 billion unique addresses. As you can imagine, we're running out!
To solve the address shortage, we have IPv6. It uses 128 bits, giving us an astronomical number of addresses. They look a bit more complex:
IPv6 is designed to support the massive growth of connected devices!
How Requests Travel: The TCP/IP Model
When you send a request (like visiting a website), it doesn't just magically appear. It goes through a series of steps, often described by the TCP/IP model.
Let's imagine you want to access a website. Here's a simplified visual of what happens:
Essentially, your request is broken down into smaller pieces called packets. Each packet has information about where it came from and where it's going (IP addresses!).
Packets are like individual envelopes carrying parts of your message.
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) vs. UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
When sending these packets, we often use TCP or UDP. They have different approaches:

• TCP: Reliable and ordered. It makes sure all packets arrive and are put back in the right order. Great for web browsing, email.
  • UDP: Faster but less reliable. It doesn't guarantee delivery or order. Good for streaming and online gaming where speed is key.
Why This is Crucial in System Design
Understanding how networks function is fundamental to building robust and efficient systems. It impacts:

• Scalability: How well your system can handle more users and data.
  • Performance: How quickly users can access your services.
  • Reliability: How often your system is available and data is not lost.
  • Security: Protecting data as it travels across networks.
By mastering these networking concepts, you can design systems that are not only functional but also performant and resilient!
